list.listitem: Although status epilepticus is traditionally defined as a seizure lasting more than 30 minutes, or repeated seizures between which consciousness is not fully regained, any seizure lasting more than 5 minutes is unlikely to cease spontaneously and treatment should begin as for status epilepticus. C
Initial management should be: airway, breathing, and circulation (ABC), check glucose level, and give glucose and thiamine. C
First-line treatment is IV lorazepam or IM midazolam. A
Second-line treatment is IV anti-epileptic drugs (eg, fosphenytoin, phenytoin) and third-line treatment is general anesthesia (involve anesthetic team early). C

background.definition: Status epilepticus is an epileptic seizure, of any type, lasting more than 30 minutes or serial seizures between which the patient fails to regain consciousness. This includes nonconvulsive status epilepticus and psychogenic nonepileptic status epilepticus.

list.listitem: Approximately 50% occur in individuals without a history of epilepsy.
10 to 60/100,000 persons per year.
Highest in infants younger than 1 year and patients older than 65 years.
Infection complicated by fever (most common cause in children)
CNS infection
Stroke (ischemic or hemorrhagic)
Metabolic derangements
Hypoxia
Eclampsia
Alcohol intoxication and withdrawal
Withdrawal of anti-epileptic drugs in patients with pre-existing epilepsy (a systematic review was unable to identify an optimal tapering regimen)
Any seizure lasting longer than 5 minutes is unlikely to cease spontaneously and will likely progress, if untreated, to status epilepticus. C

Evaluate blood glucose levels or presumptively treat seizures of unknown cause with IV glucose and thiamine to rule out hypoglycemia as a cause. Thiamine should be co-administered to prevent inadvertent iatrogenic thiamine deficiency and subsequent Wernicke's encephalopathy. C
Diagnosis of convulsive status epilepticus is clinical, while the diagnosis of nonconvulsive status epilepticus is much more dependent on EEG findings and response to treatment. C
Psychogenic nonepileptic status epilepticus must be considered in the differential diagnosis (). C

Differential.Differential_Features: Typical EEG pattern of continuous or recurrent, generalized or focal, epileptiform activity, with wide-ranging alterations in mental state

list.listitem: Initial assessment is crucial to identify the cause. History should include history from family/caregivers, including previously unrecognized seizure activity, withdrawal of anti-epilepsy drugs or decreased regimen adherence, alcohol or drug use, and past medical history.

Focal onset seizures and seizures associated with new, persistent focal deficits are more likely to be caused by an intracranial lesion (eg, tumor, stroke, abscess, or vascular malformation). Full neurologic examination should be performed in all cases and should include developmental assessment in children.

The diagnosis of nonconvulsive or subtle convulsive status epilepticus relies much more on the identification of typical EEG changes and observing response to treatment, since the clinical presentation may be a mix of altered behavior and consciousness.

Psychogenic nonconvulsive status epilepticus occurs more frequently in female, adolescent, and young adult patients. It is characterized by atypical seizure features such as eye closure, back arching, side-to-side ("no-no") head shaking and wild, asynchronous flailing of the arms and pelvis (see ). These patients more frequently have port systems implanted, require higher doses of benzodiazepines before cessation or respiratory failure, and have lower serum creatine kinase levels.
To rule out treatable causes, consider giving glucose together with thiamine immediately.

Perform the following initial tests: CBC and complete metabolic profile; urinalysis; c-reactive protein test; coagulation studies; magnesium, B12, and folate levels; toxicology; blood cultures; and ABG test.
Evaluate anticonvulsant levels in patients already taking them.
All women of childbearing age should have a pregnancy test performed to guide anticonvulsant choice and rule out eclampsia.
Where possible, neuroimaging should take place in the emergency department. After neuroimaging, consider a lumbar puncture, if clinically indicated, especially if patient is immunocompromised.

Consider EEG in all patients, especially if you suspect nonconvulsive status epilepticus, to confirm adequacy of treatment following cessation of clinically overt convulsive movements, and to exclude subtle convulsive status epilepticus in those who have received long-acting paralytics or are in a drug-induced coma. See 5-stage serial EEG changes in .
Point of care EEG is a low cost 2 channel device that has been shown to be effective in pilot studies at detecting nonconvulsive status epilepticus in children.

Elevated serum prolactin levels (2-fold higher than normal when obtained 10-20 minutes after the event) can be used as an adjunct to diagnosis in adults and older children (sensitivity is 46% for partial and 60% for generalized tonic-clonic seizure, specificity is 96%; LR+ 11/15, LR− 0.6/0.4). It does not differentiate epileptic seizures from syncope and its role has not been established in the evaluation of status epilepticus, recurrent seizures, or in neonates.

Status epilepticus is a prolonged seizure that risks airway compromise, injury, and neuronal damage. Seizures lasting more than 5 minutes will likely not cease spontaneously and are indicative of status epilepticus.
See for approach to these prolonged seizures.
The initial treatment is stabilization of vital functions (airways, breathing, circulation). C
First-line treatment should be IM midazolam or IV lorazepam rather than diazepam to control seizures. A
Second-line treatment: fosphenytoin, phenytoin, or valproate. C
Third-line treatment: general anesthesia (eg, propofol, thiopental). C
See the approach to treatment in . The aim of treatment is to shorten seizure length with the use of benzodiazepines, even in the pre-hospital setting.

Lorazepam IV (0.1 mg/kg as a slow bolus, usually 4 mg) should be used as first-line treatment rather than diazepam IV (0.15 mg/kg, usually 10 mg). This is based largely on a well-designed RCT that compared lorazepam, diazepam followed by phenytoin, phenytoin alone, and phenobarbital in 570 patients with status epilepticus. A systematic review found that compared with diazepam, lorazepam reduces the likelihood of seizure noncessation (RR 0.64; 95% CI, 0.45-0.88) and reduces the likelihood of requiring additional drugs or general anesthesia (RR 0.63; 95% CI, 0.45-0.88). It was also more effective than phenytoin.

Lorazepam and diazepam may be administered rectally; there is limited evidence that lorazepam is more effective than diazepam when administered via this route. Midazolam administered buccally, nasally, or intramuscularly is an alternative.
A well-designed RCT and a systematic review concluded that midazolam IM was non-inferior to lorazepam IV in seizure cessation and may be easier to administer in prehospital settings.
Respiratory depression and hypotension can occur with all benzodiazepines, therefore patients should be monitored for such signs.
Although phenytoin is commonly used prior to other anti-epileptic drugs for second-line treatment, valproate and levetiracetam may be more effective.
Two open-label RCTs found that levetiracetam was as effective as phenytoin for status epilepticus in children and easier to administer.

A systematic review of 15 studies concluded that seizure termination was higher for levetiracetam than for phenytoin (76.9% vs 70.5%, p = 0.005) and that the incidence of recurrence within 24 hours was lower for levetiracetam (10% vs 15.6%, p < 0.001).

A systematic review concluded that adding levetiracetam to clonazepam is no better than clonazepam alone, and based on a single trial at high risk of bias phenobarbital plus optional phenytoin may be more effective than diazepam plus phenytoin.

Ketamine is an option for add-on therapy in patients with status epilepticus refractory to midazolam, especially in the pre-hospital setting. An out-of-hospital study used propensity score matching in a before-after design to compare 2 doses of midazolam with midazolam followed by ketamine. The latter group had a higher rate of resolution (94.4% vs 82.0%) prior to hospital arrival.

A network meta-analysis identified 16 studies for treatment of benzodiazepine resistant status epilepticus. It concluded that phenobarbital and high dose levetiracetam were more effective than phenytoin for the outcome of seizure termination within 60 minutes. However, phenobarbital also had a higher risk for intubation and cardiovascular instability. A second network meta-analysis with 7 RCTs with 780 patients had a similar conclusion.
Although general anesthesia is typically reserved for third-line treatment, it may be used instead of second-line treatments (see ).

A systematic review identified only very low certainty evidence for perampanel, a selective, noncompetitive alpha-amino-3-hydroxy-5-methyl-4-isoxazolepropionic (AMPA) receptor antagonist, for the treatment of refractory and super-refractory status epilepticus.

The goal of treatment of typical absence nonconvulsive status epilepticus and complex-partial nonconvulsive status epilepticus with known epilepsy is to stabilize vital signs and reduce injury with the use of oral, rather than IV benzodiazepines, when possible; the effect on neuronal damage is not known.
Patients in nonconvulsive status epilepticus in coma may require more aggressive treatment, in an attempt to improve a markedly poor prognosis.
Resective surgery (eg, of a space-occupying lesion) and brain stimulation may be used in selected patients.
A case report described successful treatment of a patient with super refractory status epilepticus treated with responsive neurostimulation combined with surgical resection.
All patients with suspected status epilepticus should be transferred to a hospital, ideally following stabilization and the administration of first-line benzodiazepines.
The prognosis is widely variable depending on patient age, seizure type (worse with myoclonic), duration (especially if >24 hours), and underlying pathology (3%-25% mortality). B

The standardized mortality ratio compared with age-matched controls is only 1.1 (95% CI, 0.5-2.3) for idiopathic status epilepticus but is 3.0 to 3.8 for all other causes. The overall mortality in a series of 184 patients surviving at least 30 days after status epilepticus was 40%. B
EEG findings may be of prognostic significance. B
Recurrence rates based on data from two randomized trials are between 10% and 20%. B
The risk of status epilepticus is twice as high in patients older than 65 years as in younger patients. Nonconvulsive status epilepticus may be more common, but is more difficult to diagnose.

Status epilepticus is due to cerebrovascular disease in 60% of patients, with 2 times greater mortality overall and 3 times greater mortality if associated with ischemic stroke. Overall mortality is 38%, but closer to 50% if the patient is older than 80 years.
Elderly patients may require prolonged EEG monitoring since older persons are more likely to have nondiagnostic changes.

Approximately 55% of patients with convulsive status epilepticus respond to benzodiazepines, 14.9% if subtle status epilepticus. Lorazepam may be more effective than other anticonvulsants in older patients.
Patients with refractory status epilepticus should be treated with general anesthesia with continuous EEG monitoring.
All women of childbearing age should have a pregnancy test because of the risk of eclampsia as an underlying diagnosis and with regard to antiepileptic drug choice to avoid teratogenicity.

A Cochrane review of four studies with 383 children in acute tonic-clonic convulsion including status epilepticus concluded that IV lorazepam is the preferred agent. Buccal midazolam is an option if IV access is not available.

cell.label: Initial assessment (ABCs), secure airway, give oxygen, IV access, and blood work.
IV lorazepam (0.1 mg/kg), repeat after 10-20 minutes. If malnourished/alcoholic consider IV dextrose and thiamine.
Phenytoin (15-18 mg/kg at 50 mg/min) and/or phenobarbital (10-15 mg/kg at 100 mg/min). Alert anesthesist, ECG monitoring.
General anesthesia; taper off general anesthesia 12-24 hours after last seizure.
Give usual anti-epileptic drugs and monitor patient closely.
Consider and treat causes and complications; consider neuroimaging.
Intensive care, ECG monitoring; intracranial pressure monitoring as appropriate, start long-term anti-epileptic drugs.

feature.caption: Distinguishing Epileptic Seizure from Psychogenic Nonepileptic Status Epilepticus (PNESE).
feature.feature_body:
Epileptic Seizure PNESE
Precipitant Rare Common, emotion/stress
When alone/asleep Common May be reported
Onset Short Short or several minutes
Aura Various, stereotyped Fear, panic, altered mental state
Eyes Open Closed
Speech Cry, grunt, muttering, autosomatisms Semi-voluntary, often unintelligible
Movement Atonic, tonic, clonic small amplitude Asynchronous, pelvic thrusting, opisthotonus
Injury Tongue biting, fall May bite or fall, directed violence not uncommon
Consciousness Complete or incomplete loss Variable, inconsistent
Stimulation None in general, may respond in complex partial Often responds, may terminate seizure
Incontinence Common Sometimes
